items.title: L12: Reading a Grade 7 advert
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: A Grade 7 advert asks for a different kind of evidence from a HEO or SEO one. The behaviours are normally assessed at the fourth level, where Leadership means leading through other managers, Communicating and Influencing involves shaping the views of senior stakeholders, and Seeing the Big Picture means linking your work to the department's wider priorities and the policy or delivery environment. Look for signals of scale in the advert: the size of the team and whether you would manage managers, the size of a budget, the number of external partners, ministerial or senior leadership contact, and whether the post carries accountability for a service or a policy area. A Grade 7 post often expects you to set direction and decide priorities, not only to deliver them. The sift may ask for fewer, deeper examples than at lower grades, and the panel is looking for outcomes, your personal contribution and the judgement you exercised when the right answer was unclear. If your current experience is at SEO level, you can apply where you can show that you have already led across teams, handled ambiguity and influenced beyond your own line. Some Grade 7 posts are in a profession, such as digital, data, finance or legal, and then technical or professional requirements carry more weight. Read the advert for what is essential and what is desirable, and be honest about where you meet the standard only partly, because the interview will test it.

questions.prompt: At which behaviour level are Grade 7 posts normally assessed?

options.text: The fourth level, above the one used for HEO and SEO
The second level, as Grade 7 posts are specialist
The same third level as HEO and SEO
The fifth level, which is used for most senior posts

questions.hint: Grade 7 and 6 are usually assessed one level above HEO and SEO.

questions.prompt: How does Leadership at the Grade 7 level differ from the HEO or SEO level?

options.text: It centres on directly supervising a single small team of staff
It centres on following direction closely while delivering to deadlines
It centres on leading through other managers and across teams
It centres on representing the department in public on all occasions

questions.hint: Higher levels involve leading through others.

questions.prompt: Which advert signal best suggests that a post carries real Grade 7 scale?

options.text: A closing date several weeks away from the advert date
A request for a CV and a personal statement of any length
A location in the department's headquarters building
Managing managers and a significant budget or service

questions.hint: Scale shows in teams, budgets, partners and accountability.

questions.prompt: A Grade 7 sift asks for fewer examples than a HEO one. What does this usually mean for your answers?

options.text: Each example should describe the team's work without naming your own part
Each example should be deeper, showing outcomes, your contribution and judgement
Each example can be shorter and less detailed because less is expected at this grade
Each example should list as many tasks as possible within the word count

questions.hint: Fewer examples means more depth is expected from each.

questions.prompt: Which type of evidence is most distinctive at Grade 7?

options.text: Completing assigned tasks accurately within a short time limit
Attending a high number of meetings across several departments
Following guidance closely on every occasion without deviation
Setting direction and deciding priorities when the answer is unclear

questions.hint: Higher grades set direction and exercise judgement under ambiguity.

questions.prompt: You are an SEO and want to apply for Grade 7. Which approach is most credible?

options.text: Wait until you have held the SEO grade for a minimum number of years
Show you have already led across teams and handled ambiguity
Apply only to posts that are described as development posts
Describe your SEO duties in detail and let the panel infer the rest

questions.hint: Credibility comes from evidence of Grade 7-level behaviour, not time served.

questions.prompt: A Grade 7 post is in a profession such as finance or data. What usually carries more weight?

options.text: Willingness to move department if asked in future
Personal interest in the profession's history
Technical or professional requirements alongside behaviours
Length of service in the Civil Service as a whole

questions.hint: Professional posts weight technical and professional standards.

questions.prompt: An advert lists some criteria as essential and others as desirable. How should you treat them?

options.text: Meet the essentials and be honest about partial matches
Concentrate on desirable criteria because they distinguish candidates
Ignore desirable criteria entirely because panels never mark them
Treat both lists as optional and apply regardless of the match

questions.hint: Essential criteria must be met; desirable ones add weight.

questions.prompt: Which phrase in a Grade 7 advert most clearly signals accountability?

options.text: You will be expected to support colleagues as required
You will have regular contact with colleagues across the building
You will be given training in the department's systems
You will be accountable for delivering a service

questions.hint: Accountability for a service or policy area is a hallmark of senior posts.

questions.prompt: Why can it be a mistake to describe teamwork in the plural throughout a Grade 7 example?

options.text: Group examples are not allowed in Success Profile assessments
The panel scores your own contribution and decisions, not the group's
Plurals are marked down as informal language in sift answers
Panels are not interested in how teams work together at this grade

questions.hint: Panels score what you did personally.

items.title: L12: Writing a HEO-level personal statement
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: A personal statement is a written answer, usually with a word limit, that shows how your experience meets the person specification. At HEO level, a strong statement is organised around the criteria the advert says will be scored, not around your career history. A common structure is to open briefly with why you are applying, then give one or two examples per behaviour, each following a clear sequence: the situation, what you were responsible for, the specific actions you took, and the result, including a measure where you have one. The actions are the heart of the answer, written in the first person so that the panel can see what you did. Avoid long descriptions of context, because a sift scorer has to cover many statements and rewards clarity. Stay within the word limit, since statements that exceed it may be cut off or marked down. Use plain language and explain any department-specific acronyms. At HEO level, show that you led or coordinated the work, made a judgement, and influenced others, not only that you carried out tasks. Where the advert asks for particular behaviours, make sure the example really shows that behaviour: an example about a deadline that was met by working late shows commitment but not necessarily Delivering at Pace in the Success Profile sense. Check facts, because claims can be tested at interview and false claims can lead to withdrawal of an offer. Ask someone to read the draft, and proofread it carefully for errors.

questions.prompt: How should a strong personal statement be organised?

options.text: Around the department's mission statement and values
Around the sections of your current job description
Around the criteria that the advert says will be scored
In chronological order of your career history

questions.hint: A statement is scored on the criteria, so it should follow them.

questions.prompt: Which element of a worked example carries most weight with a scorer?

options.text: The specific actions you took, written in the first person
A summary of what your manager thought of you
A list of the people involved in the project
A detailed description of the context and background

questions.prompt: Why avoid long descriptions of context in a statement?

options.text: The panel already knows your department's work in full
Long context sections cause the form to be rejected by the system
Scorers read many statements and reward clear evidence
Context is considered confidential and cannot be disclosed

questions.hint: Brevity about context leaves room for evidence.

questions.prompt: What risk do you run by exceeding a stated word limit?

options.text: The sift panel will ask you to resubmit within a day
The application will be moved to a different competition
The statement will be given extra weight for detail
The statement may be cut off or marked down

questions.hint: Limits exist to keep scoring fair.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows HEO-level behaviour?

options.text: You attended a series of training courses relevant to the post
You coordinated a team, made a priority judgement and influenced a stakeholder
You carried out a series of tasks accurately and on time as instructed
You supported a manager who led a high-profile piece of work

questions.hint: HEO examples show leading, judging and influencing.

questions.prompt: An applicant writes that they met a deadline by working late and says this shows Delivering at Pace. What is the weakness?

options.text: It shows effort but not necessarily planning and prioritising
It would be accepted only if the deadline was set by a minister
It is irrelevant because Delivering at Pace is never assessed at HEO
It shows no effort, so the scorer cannot give credit

questions.hint: The behaviour is about planning and prioritising, not long hours alone.

questions.prompt: Why should you explain department-specific acronyms?

options.text: Acronyms are banned from statements by the Recruitment Principles
The scorer may be from elsewhere in government
The system rejects statements containing unexplained capitals
The panel scores acronyms as technical content

questions.prompt: What happens to a claim in your statement that cannot be supported?

options.text: It will be corrected by the panel before scoring
It will be treated as an honest mistake whatever the circumstances
It will be ignored since only the interview is scored
It can be tested at interview and may lead to an offer being withdrawn

questions.hint: Claims must be accurate and verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which opening is most useful in a personal statement?

options.text: A short reason for applying, then straight into evidence
A full account of your career since you joined
A request that the panel treat your answer sympathetically
A summary of the department's recent achievements

questions.hint: A short opening leaves space for evidence.

questions.prompt: Why ask someone to read your draft before you submit?

options.text: It removes the need for you to proofread the final version
A reader's comments are scored as part of your evidence
A fresh reader can spot unclear actions, errors and missed criteria
Panels require a named reader's confirmation on each statement

items.title: L12: Strengths-based versus competency-style interviews
items.body: Civil Service interviews often mix two styles of question. Behaviour or competency questions ask for evidence of past action: tell us about a time you led a team through change. The best answers describe a specific situation, what you were responsible for, what you did and the result, and they are scored against the behaviour at the grade level. Strengths-based questions are different. They ask what you enjoy and do well and are usually shorter and more spontaneous, such as which tasks give you energy or what you would do first with an unfamiliar problem. They are not looking for a rehearsed story, and some strengths questions have no right or wrong answer; the panel looks for energy, authenticity and a pattern across your answers. Typical signals include how quickly you respond, whether you talk with enthusiasm, whether you give examples when asked and how well your responses fit the role. Preparation is still useful: reflect on your own strengths, read the strengths named in the advert and rehearse speaking about them naturally. Do not try to guess the answer that a panel wants, because strengths are assessed for fit, and inconsistent answers show. For competency questions, prepare more than one example for each behaviour so that you are not caught out when a question overlaps with a previous answer. If you do not know an answer, say so and explain how you would approach it, which is better than inventing a story.

questions.prompt: Which describes a behaviour or competency question?

options.text: A question about your opinions of the department
A request for evidence of something you did in the past
A question about what you enjoy doing most
A request to summarise the person specification

questions.hint: Behaviour questions ask for past evidence.

questions.prompt: What is a strengths-based question designed to reveal?

options.text: What you do well and enjoy, shown through energy and authenticity
How long you have spent in your current post and how often you move
How closely you have memorised the wording of the advert
Which answers the panel would most like to hear on the day

questions.hint: Strengths questions look for natural energy and fit.

questions.prompt: Why are strengths questions usually shorter and more spontaneous?

options.text: They replace the need for a competency section
They are scored against a fixed list of correct answers
They look for natural responses rather than a rehearsed story
They are designed to catch candidates who are unprepared

questions.prompt: How should you approach a strengths question?

options.text: Give the answer you think the panel prefers
Refuse to answer if you have no strong view
Repeat the wording of the advert as closely as possible
Answer naturally and honestly rather than guess what the panel wants

questions.hint: Panels assess fit, so inconsistent answers show.

questions.prompt: What is the best structure for a competency answer?

options.text: A summary of your CV in date order with the most recent role first
Situation, your responsibility, what you did and the result
A list of the personal qualities you believe you have, with some examples
A description of what the whole team achieved, with names of colleagues

questions.hint: Evidence of action and result is scored.

questions.prompt: Why prepare more than one example for each behaviour?

options.text: The panel scores the number of examples rather than their quality
Panels always ask for exactly two examples per behaviour
A later question may overlap and you will need an alternative
Examples used in the sift cannot be repeated at all

questions.hint: Spare examples prevent being caught out.

questions.prompt: A candidate cannot answer a technical question. Which response is best?

options.text: Say so and explain how you would go about finding the answer
Invent a plausible account of what you have done
Ask the panel to move to the next question without explanation
Change the subject to a related topic you know well

questions.hint: Honesty and approach are better than invention.

questions.prompt: Which feature is a typical signal in a strengths answer?

options.text: A reference to the competition's closing date in your opening
A formal and even tone from the start to the end of the interview
The use of a long list of qualifications in each answer you give
Energy and enthusiasm when you speak about the topic

questions.hint: Panels look for energy and authenticity.

questions.prompt: Which statement about preparing for strengths questions is most accurate?

options.text: Preparation is needed only for external candidates
Preparation helps you reflect on genuine strengths and speak naturally
Preparation is pointless since answers cannot be improved
Preparation means rehearsing exact scripts for each answer

questions.prompt: A panel notices that your answers on what you enjoy contradict each other. What is the likely effect?

options.text: It will be scored as evidence that you are adaptable in different settings
It will be ignored because strengths answers are not scored at all
It can suggest the answers are not authentic and weaken the fit assessment
It will lead to automatic disqualification from the competition

items.title: L12: Evidencing the Experience and Technical elements
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: Two Success Profile elements rely less on how you behave and more on what you have, so they need a different style of evidence. Experience asks whether you have the knowledge or mastery of an activity or subject gained through study, work or other life experience. Technical asks whether you hold the specific skills, qualifications or professional standards the job needs. For Experience, panels want relevant, recent and sufficiently complex examples: the type of work, the scale, the context and what you learnt. A long period in a post is not proof of experience in a particular activity, and a short period can provide depth if the work was demanding. For Technical, the advert will often list qualifications or standards, such as a recognised accountancy qualification or a project management or digital or data standard. If a qualification is essential, you normally must hold it or be in the process of obtaining it where the advert says so. Evidence may include certificates, membership of a professional body, a record of continuing professional development or a work sample. Be precise: state the qualification, the awarding body and the date. If the advert says equivalent experience will be considered, explain why your experience is equivalent rather than assuming it. Where technical skills are assessed by a task, such as a written exercise or data analysis, practise under similar conditions. Do not overstate your level: if you have used a tool, say how and for what, because specific claims can be tested.

questions.prompt: Which Success Profile element asks about knowledge or mastery gained through study, work or life?

options.text: Experience
Ability
Strengths
Technical

questions.hint: That is the definition of Experience.

questions.prompt: What do panels typically look for when assessing Experience?

options.text: The number of departments you have worked in
The longest possible period in post
A list of every task you have done
Relevant, recent examples of sufficient complexity

questions.hint: Quality and relevance matter more than length.

questions.prompt: Is a long period in a post proof of experience in a specific activity?

options.text: A long period alone does not prove experience of a particular activity
A long period proves it only for civil servants
A long period proves experience of everything in the post
A long period is the only evidence panels accept

questions.hint: Time in post is not the same as relevant depth.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a Technical element?

options.text: Willingness to work flexible hours for as long as the post requires
Enthusiasm for the department's mission and the work it carries out
A recognised project management or accountancy qualification
Experience of leading a team through a period of organisational change

questions.hint: Technical covers specific skills and qualifications.

questions.prompt: An advert lists a qualification as essential. What does that normally mean?

options.text: It will be waived if you perform well enough at the interview
You must hold it, or be working towards it where the advert allows
You may ignore it if you have longer service than other applicants
You will be given credit for any similar course you have taken

questions.hint: Essential means required unless stated otherwise.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the best way to evidence a qualification?

options.text: Say that you hold a relevant qualification without details
Say that you are interested in gaining it later
Say that you studied the subject at some point
Name the qualification, the awarding body and the date obtained

questions.prompt: An advert says equivalent experience will be considered. What should you do?

options.text: Assume equivalence and say nothing about it
Explain why your experience is equivalent rather than assuming it
Ask the panel to decide at interview without information
Apply only if you hold the exact qualification

questions.prompt: How should you prepare for a technical task such as a written exercise?

options.text: Ask the panel for the task in advance so that you can prepare fully
Practise only on easy examples so that your confidence stays high
Read about the task's author and the style in which it is usually set
Practise under similar conditions, including the time limit

questions.hint: Realistic practice builds skill and timing.

questions.prompt: Why avoid overstating your level with a tool or method?

options.text: Claims can be tested at interview or in the job
Overstating is not scored
Overstating is encouraged to stand out
Panels do not ask about tools

questions.hint: Specific claims must be backed by real competence.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best supports a professional membership claim?

options.text: A note of the courses you intend to take
A statement that colleagues think you are skilled
A membership number or certificate and date of admission
A reference from a friend in the profession

items.title: L12: Choosing between internal-only and open competitions
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Recruitment Principles
items.body: When you are a serving civil servant looking to move up, each advert gives a different mix of opportunity and risk, and the eligibility wording shapes your strategy. A competition open to civil servants in your department only is the narrowest pool, so you face fewer rivals, but the posts are often fewer and the competition can be intense among people who know each other. A competition open to civil servants across government widens the pool and the destinations, which helps if you want to change department. An open competition draws external applicants, who may have strong specialist experience, and so may be tougher in areas such as digital or commercial work; but it also offers more posts, often at higher grades. Do not rely on one route. A sensible approach is to track adverts in all three, apply where you can honestly meet the essential criteria and keep your evidence ready. Be aware that your terms and conditions can differ depending on the route: a civil servant moving between departments usually keeps their continuous service, while an external appointee does not. Priority is not given to internal candidates in an open competition: everyone is assessed on merit. Some roles are advertised as open to all but give existing civil servants practical advantages such as knowledge of systems or networks, which are not criteria. Check the wording, such as civil servants only or open to the public, because applying where you are not eligible can lose time and credibility.

questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off of a competition limited to your own department?

options.text: Fewer rivals, but often fewer posts and strong competition from colleagues who know the work
A quicker move to the top of the pay range for whoever wins
Many more rivals, but a guaranteed interview for every member of staff in the department
A higher grade offered to every candidate who passes the sift

questions.hint: Narrow pools reduce rivals but also options.

questions.prompt: Why might an across-government competition suit you if you want to change department?

options.text: It guarantees a move to the department you rank first when you apply
It removes the need for a panel, as civil servants are already vetted
It widens destinations while limiting rivals to civil servants
It gives priority to applicants with the longest continuous service

questions.hint: It broadens destinations within the Civil Service.

questions.prompt: How might external applicants affect an open competition?

options.text: They cannot be appointed to posts above HEO in any department
They may bring strong specialist experience, so the field can be tougher in some areas
They are scored lower on every criterion because they lack departmental knowledge
They are only considered once all civil service applicants have been assessed

questions.hint: Specialist external candidates can be strong competitors.

questions.prompt: Which strategy is most sensible for a serving civil servant who wants to move up?

options.text: Apply only to open competitions, since these always carry the highest salaries
Apply only within your own department, where you are already known and trusted
Wait for a vacancy to be circulated to you personally before applying
Track all three advert types and apply wherever you honestly meet the essentials

questions.hint: Do not rely on one route.

questions.prompt: A civil servant and an external appointee both join the same department. What may differ?

options.text: A civil servant often keeps continuous service, an external appointee starts afresh
The external appointee always receives a longer notice period
The civil servant is always paid less because of existing pay history
The civil servant cannot negotiate pay on appointment at all

questions.prompt: In an open competition, how are existing civil servants treated at assessment?

options.text: They are scored first and others only if posts remain unfilled
They are exempt from the interview because their record is known
They are assessed on merit against the same criteria as everyone else
They receive bonus marks for knowing how the department works

questions.prompt: Which of these is a real advantage for internal candidates but NOT a scoring criterion?

options.text: Evidence that you meet the essential criteria of the post, shown in your answers
Performance at the online tests and interview in the competition
Meeting the stated technical requirement set out in the advert
Knowing the department's systems and having a network of colleagues

questions.hint: Familiarity helps but is not scored.

questions.prompt: Why should you check wording such as civil servants only or open to the public before applying?

options.text: The wording determines the salary you will be offered on appointment
Applying where you are ineligible wastes time and can damage your credibility
The wording decides which panel members will score your application
The wording decides whether the post is permanent or fixed term

questions.prompt: You are an HEO who wants a same-grade move to a different department. Which advert type is the most direct route?

options.text: An across-government or open vacancy at HEO that interests you
A department-only vacancy in your own department at HEO
A temporary promotion offer in your current team
A reserve list from a competition you did not enter

questions.hint: Cross-department posts are in across-government or open adverts.

questions.prompt: A role is open to all and you know the internal systems well. How should you build your application?

options.text: Focus on how long you have served rather than on outcomes
Leave out detail on the work you have done because the panel already knows it
Assume the panel will credit your inside knowledge and keep answers brief
Evidence the stated criteria directly, since familiarity is not scored

items.title: L12: Secondment and loan agreements in practice
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; departmental HR policy
items.body: A loan or secondment is only as good as its agreement, and the details determine whether it helps your career. A sound agreement usually covers the start and end dates, the purpose and nature of the work, the host line manager, who pays salary and other costs, how performance will be managed and recorded, working location and hours, and what happens if either party wants to end the arrangement early. It should say what happens at the end: return to the home post, extension by agreement or, where there is a competition, the chance to apply for a permanent post on equal terms. Consider your substantive post carefully. Some departments hold the post open; others backfill it with a temporary appointment, which can complicate your return. Ask your home manager how your performance will be assessed for pay and promotion purposes, because host managers often write the reports but the home department makes the decisions. Check that your pension and continuous service are unaffected. If you move to a body outside the Civil Service, your terms may vary and your Civil Service Code obligations and confidentiality duties still apply as the agreement provides. Think about visibility: stay in touch with your home department so that you are not forgotten when vacancies arise. An agreement is a negotiated document: ask questions early, put the answers in writing and keep a copy.

questions.prompt: Which items should a sound secondment or loan agreement cover?

options.text: A guarantee of promotion on return to the home department
Start and end dates, the host line manager, who pays and how performance is managed
A summary of the host organisation's recent financial results
The names of the other candidates who were considered for the opportunity

questions.prompt: What should an agreement say about the end of the period?

options.text: That you will be promoted at the host when the period ends
That you may not discuss the work you did once it is over
Whether you return to your home post, extend or can compete for a permanent one
That you must resign from your home department to stay on

questions.prompt: Why ask how your home department will assess your performance during a loan?

options.text: Host managers alone decide the pay of every seconded person
Host managers write reports, but home departments usually decide pay and promotion
Performance reports from loans are not used in promotion decisions
Home departments never take account of performance on a loan

questions.hint: Know how evidence will be used.

questions.prompt: What is one risk if your home post is backfilled while you are away?

options.text: You are promoted automatically into the backfilled post
You lose your continuous service as soon as you leave
Your pay is paid by both organisations at once
Return can be complicated if the temporary holder remains in post

questions.prompt: Which question about terms matters most before accepting a secondment?

options.text: Whether your pension and continuous service stay unaffected
Whether the host's building has better facilities than your own
Whether the host's pension scheme is larger than yours
Whether the host's logo is more widely known

questions.prompt: You are seconded to a body outside the Civil Service. Which duties may still apply?

options.text: Only the host's internal policies and nothing from your home department
Duties lapse for the period, since you are temporarily outside the Civil Service
Civil Service Code and confidentiality duties, as the agreement provides
Only duties about pay and working time

questions.prompt: How can you stay visible to your home department while away?

options.text: Withdraw from contact so the host sees your full commitment
Ask the host to write to every panel that you apply to
Rely on the host to lobby for your return to a higher grade
Keep in touch so you are considered when vacancies arise

questions.prompt: Who normally shapes the terms of a loan or secondment?

options.text: The selection panel that chose you for the opportunity
The Cabinet Office centrally, which sets one standard form
You, your home manager and the host, recorded in writing
The Civil Service Commission, which approves every agreement

questions.hint: An agreement is negotiated and recorded.

questions.prompt: At the end of a loan, what is true about a permanent post at the host?

options.text: There is no automatic right to one without a fair and open competition
You are entitled to it if you have worked there for more than a year
You are entitled to it if the lending department agrees
You are entitled to the permanent post if the host wants you

questions.prompt: Either party wants to end a secondment early. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Ask the Civil Service Commission to decide the matter
Follow the procedure set out in the agreement
Wait until the end date regardless of the circumstances
Simply stop attending on the date you prefer

items.title: L12: Agreeing acting-up terms in writing
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; departmental HR policy
items.body: Acting up is easy to agree in a corridor conversation and hard to sort out afterwards, so the terms should be written down. A sound agreement identifies the higher post, the start date and a clear end date or review point, and states the reason for the arrangement, such as maternity cover, a vacancy or a project. It says how you were chosen: was it an open expression of interest, a short assessment or a direct appointment on a short-term basis? It sets out the pay you will receive for the period and when it starts, and how it is calculated, noting that departmental practice varies. It confirms that your substantive grade and post continue and that you return to them when the period ends. It sets out the authority you hold, such as budget or line management, and who you report to. It should also state who will assess your performance and how the evidence will be recorded, because that evidence will later support your case for promotion. If the arrangement is likely to run beyond a short period, ask about the plan to fill the post permanently, since leaving it open can attract fairness concerns. Do not treat a verbal promise of the permanent job as binding: appointments must follow fair and open competition. Keep copies of the agreement and any extensions, and ask for any change in writing.

questions.prompt: Why should acting-up terms be put in writing?

options.text: A written agreement makes the permanent post yours
Pension rules require every arrangement to be signed
Verbal arrangements are easy to dispute later
Written terms are the only way to receive higher pay

questions.prompt: Which items belong in an acting-up agreement?

options.text: A list of the colleagues who were not selected
A clear end date or review point and the reason for the arrangement
A forecast of next year's budget for the team
A guarantee that you will be appointed permanently at the end

questions.hint: Time limit and purpose are essential.

questions.prompt: Why record how you were chosen for the acting role?

options.text: It guarantees you an interview for the permanent post when it is advertised
It determines your pay band for the rest of your career in the department
It sets the pension entitlement you will receive for the period
It shows the selection was transparent and helps answer fairness concerns

questions.prompt: What should be clear about pay in the agreement?

options.text: What you will be paid, when it starts and how it is worked out
That pay will be set by the host team at its discretion
That pay will be decided after the period has ended
That pay will stay at your substantive grade throughout

questions.prompt: What should the agreement confirm about your substantive grade?

options.text: That it is suspended and cannot be restored
That it continues and you return to it when the period ends
That it is replaced permanently by the higher grade
That it is surrendered for the duration of the arrangement

questions.hint: Acting up does not change substantive grade.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter who assesses your performance while acting up?

options.text: The assessor selects the interview panel for the permanent post
The assessor chooses the person who gets the permanent job
The recorded evidence will later support your promotion case
The assessor sets your pay for the following year

questions.prompt: An arrangement looks likely to run on for a long time. What should you ask about?

options.text: The plan to fill the post permanently by fair and open competition
Whether colleagues need to be told about the arrangement
Whether the end date can be removed
A guarantee that you will keep the post when it is filled

questions.hint: Open-ended acting up raises fairness concerns.

questions.prompt: Your manager says the permanent post will be yours after acting up. How should you treat this?

options.text: As a reason to skip applying when the post is advertised
As a binding contract you can rely on
As evidence you can give the panel
As non-binding, since appointments follow fair and open competition

questions.hint: Verbal promises do not override competition.

questions.prompt: Your acting-up period is extended. What should you do?

options.text: Accept a verbal extension, since a written one is not needed
Assume the original terms continue indefinitely without changes
Wait to see whether your pay changes before raising anything
Ask for the extension and any change of terms in writing

questions.prompt: Which authority should the agreement set out?

options.text: The authority to promote other staff in the team without a competition
The authority to set your own pay when you return to your substantive post
The budget, line management and reporting lines that come with the higher post
The authority to choose your own successor in the acting post

items.title: L12: Competing for the permanent post you are acting in
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: Being in a post temporarily does not make you the favourite, and it brings particular risks when the permanent job is advertised. You will be assessed on the same criteria and evidence as every other candidate, and the panel must not assume that your time in the role is merit. You do hold advantages, such as recent, relevant examples and knowledge of the work, and you should use them by giving specific evidence rather than relying on the panel's impression. Beware complacency: external and other internal candidates may have stronger evidence on some criteria, and acting up can leave you with gaps if the role has narrowed your experience. You also face conflicts. If you manage the colleagues who are applying, avoid influencing the panel, and declare any relationship with panel members. You should not be involved in designing the advert or the criteria, or in shortlisting, because that would give you an unfair advantage. If you have information that is not available to other candidates, such as who has applied or the panel composition, do not use it. The Civil Service Code requires integrity and impartiality, so behave as you would want your rivals to behave. If you succeed, the appointment is made on merit, and if you do not, ask for feedback and decide whether to return to your substantive post or seek other roles. Your manager should treat you the same as other candidates throughout.

questions.prompt: Does acting in a post make you the favourite for the permanent job?

options.text: It does when the post has been vacant for a long time
It does not, because the panel must assess everyone on the same criteria and evidence
It does for the person who has worked longest in the department
It does, because experience in the role is the main criterion for selection

questions.hint: Time in the role is not merit in itself.

questions.prompt: What advantage does an acting person legitimately hold in the competition?

options.text: Recent, relevant evidence they can present in detail
A right to be shortlisted without a sift
A right to help set the criteria for the post
A right to see the other candidates' applications

questions.prompt: Why is complacency a risk for the acting person?

options.text: Other candidates may have stronger evidence on some criteria
The department may decide not to advertise the post
The post may be withdrawn if the acting person scores well
The panel may skip the interview for acting candidates

questions.hint: Competition may be stronger than expected.

questions.prompt: You manage colleagues who have also applied. What should you do?

options.text: Offer to sit on the panel since you know them best
Avoid influencing the panel and declare any relationship with panel members
Ask your colleagues to withdraw so the best candidate can win
Brief the panel on each colleague's weaknesses so it can compare fairly

questions.prompt: Which task should the acting person NOT take part in?

options.text: Preparing your own application using your evidence from the acting period
Asking for feedback after the process has ended and decisions are made
Designing the advert or criteria and shortlisting candidates
Attending your own interview along with the other shortlisted candidates

questions.hint: Involvement in design or sift gives an unfair advantage.

questions.prompt: Through your acting role you learn who else has applied. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the panel to confirm the list of applicants
Contact them to compare evidence before the interview
Share it with the team so everyone knows the competition
Not use that information in your own application or preparation

questions.prompt: Which Civil Service Code values apply to your conduct as a candidate?

options.text: Integrity and impartiality
Speed and discretion
Loyalty and seniority
Rivalry and independence

questions.hint: The Code applies to all civil servants.

questions.prompt: How should an acting person present their time in post?

options.text: As a general account of how long they have been in the role
As a reason not to be assessed on certain criteria
With specific achievements and outcomes against each criterion
As proof of seniority which panels should respect

questions.prompt: You are unsuccessful. What is the most sensible next step?

options.text: Resign from the Civil Service because the process has shown you are not wanted
Ask for feedback and decide whether to return to your substantive post or seek other roles
Lodge an appeal with the Commission straight away, whatever the grounds
Refuse to return to your substantive post until you are promoted to the higher grade

questions.prompt: How should your manager treat you during the competition?

options.text: As someone who need not take part in the competition
As a candidate who no longer has any support
As the preferred candidate, since you have been in post
In the same way as every other candidate

items.title: L12: Turning an evidence log into a criteria-matched case
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Behaviours
items.body: An evidence log is only the raw material; a promotion case needs the evidence shaped to the criteria. Begin by listing the criteria of the target role: usually a handful of behaviours and some experience or technical requirements. For each criterion, scan your log for examples that genuinely show it at the right level, and choose the strongest one or two rather than every possible one. A single example can often serve more than one criterion, but use different examples across your application where you can, because variety shows breadth. Check each chosen example for level: does it show leading, influencing and judgement at the target grade, or only competent delivery? If the evidence is only at the lower level, look for how you could stretch it, for example by taking responsibility for a bigger piece of work before you apply. Then prepare to tell the story in two forms: a written version within a word limit and a spoken version of around two or three minutes, each beginning with the situation and ending with the result and what you learnt. Attach measures when you can, such as time saved, cost, quality or customer outcome, and make sure they are accurate and attributable. Identify someone who can verify the example, since references and panels may check. Finally, keep a short gap list of criteria with weak evidence, and take action on it so that your next log entries address those gaps.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in matching an evidence log to a role?

options.text: Ask colleagues which of your stories is best
List the criteria of the target role
Rewrite your CV in date order
Choose the longest example you have

questions.prompt: How many examples should you choose for each criterion?

options.text: The strongest one or two
A different example from each year of service
Every example that might possibly fit
Only the oldest example you have

questions.prompt: Why use different examples across an application where possible?

options.text: Variety removes the need for evidence
Different examples are automatically given higher scores
Variety shows breadth of experience
Panels forbid reuse of any example

questions.prompt: What should you check about each example you choose?

options.text: Whether it is the most recent piece of work you have ever done
Whether a manager praised it at the time it was completed
Whether it already appears in your last appraisal record
Whether it shows the behaviour at the target grade level

questions.prompt: Your evidence only reaches the lower grade's level. What can you do?

options.text: Relabel your lower-level examples so that they sound like senior work
Take on a bigger piece of work before you apply
Apply anyway and hope that the panel will be generous at the sift
Ask the panel in your application to waive the criterion you cannot meet

questions.prompt: In what two forms should you prepare an important example?

options.text: A written version within a word limit and a spoken version of a few minutes
A CV entry and a covering letter that repeat each other's content
A poster for display at the team meeting and a single slide
A long formal report and a short summary email to your manager each month

questions.hint: Both written and spoken versions are needed.

questions.prompt: How should a spoken example be framed?

options.text: Start with a joke and finish with a question to the panel
Start with the result and finish with your pay
Open with the situation and close with the result and learning
Start with the grade and finish with the team size

questions.hint: Beginning and end frame the story.

questions.prompt: Why should measures in an example be accurate and attributable?

options.text: Measures are optional, so accuracy does not matter
Measures belong to the team, not to you
Measures should be rounded up to stand out
Claims can be checked and must show your own contribution

questions.prompt: Why identify someone who can verify an example?

options.text: It is a rule of the Commission
References and panels may check the evidence
The verifier scores your application
The verifier writes your answers for you

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of keeping a gap list?

options.text: To record criteria with weak evidence so that you can act on them
To compare yourself with other candidates who have applied for the role
To hand to the panel at interview, so they can see where you are weak
To list reasons not to apply for roles in which you may fail

items.title: L12: Records, declarations and panel composition
items.source: Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles; departmental recruitment guidance
items.body: Fair and open competition depends on practical discipline that a candidate rarely sees. Panels are normally made up of people who can assess the criteria, often including someone of the right grade and, in many competitions, a person from outside the immediate team. Panel members should receive guidance on assessing, scoring and avoiding bias, and many departments expect them to have completed training. They must declare any interest or relationship with a candidate, such as being a friend, relative, or recent line manager, and a person with a significant conflict should step down. Each candidate should be assessed against the same criteria using a consistent scoring approach, with notes taken at the time that link the evidence to the score. Those records matter: they show that the decision was based on merit, they support feedback, and they allow the department to respond to a complaint or a Commission inquiry. They are normally kept for a set period, which the department specifies, and are subject to data protection rules. Panel discussions are confidential, and members should not discuss candidates outside the process. Any change to the process, such as extending a deadline, should apply to all candidates. If a panel member realises they have an undeclared conflict, they should tell the chair at once. These practices help a department show that it acted in line with the Principles.

questions.prompt: Why must panel members declare relationships with candidates?

options.text: To decide who should chair the panel for the competition
To decide which candidate receives the highest score from the panel
To confirm that the panel is large enough to cover all the criteria
To prevent bias and protect the fairness of the competition

questions.prompt: What should a panel member with a significant conflict do?

options.text: Tell the candidate in advance what score they are likely to get, as a courtesy
Ask the candidate to withdraw so that the competition can continue unaffected
Step down from assessing that candidate
Mark the candidate honestly and say nothing, as the conflict does not affect the score

questions.prompt: Why are notes taken at the time of assessment?

options.text: They link evidence to the score and support feedback and complaints
They are read out to each candidate at the end of the interview as feedback
They are destroyed once scores are agreed, so that no one can challenge them
They are used to rank the panel members for their consistency of marking

questions.prompt: Which arrangement supports a fair assessment?

options.text: Different questions for each candidate, to keep each interview fresh and to test them individually
Consistent criteria and scoring for every candidate
Scores agreed between panel members before the interviews, to save time later
One senior member deciding the outcome alone, to avoid disagreement among the panel

questions.prompt: How long are recruitment records usually kept?

options.text: For exactly one year across government, whatever the department's own rules
For as long as the successful candidate remains in post, then destroyed
Only until the appointment is confirmed, since notes are then no longer needed
For a period the department specifies, subject to data protection rules

questions.prompt: Who should know the details of panel discussions?

options.text: Everyone in the department, so that colleagues can learn from the discussion
The candidates' line managers, so that they can support those who were not appointed
Only those in the process, because discussions are confidential
Anyone who asks, since recruitment decisions are public information in government

questions.prompt: The advert deadline is extended for one candidate. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Apply the extension to all candidates
Keep the original deadline for everyone else and allow the one extension quietly
Allow the extension but ask the candidate not to tell others about it
Cancel the competition and begin again with a new advert

questions.prompt: A panel member realises they have an undeclared conflict. What should they do?

options.text: Score that candidate lower than the rest to compensate for the conflict
Tell the chair at once
Withdraw from the panel without telling anyone the reason for leaving
Wait to see whether the candidate performs well enough for it to matter

questions.hint: Disclose as soon as it is known.

questions.prompt: What do good records allow a department to do?

options.text: Change scores later if a senior manager disagrees with the original outcome
Rank panel members by how closely each one's scores matched the final decision
Publish interview notes to show candidates how each answer was marked
Respond to a complaint or a Commission inquiry

questions.prompt: Which panel member would strengthen independence?

options.text: A colleague who has also applied, so there is a peer view of the field
The candidate's current line manager, who knows how they work day to day
Someone from outside the immediate team
The previous post-holder, who understands the job in detail

items.title: L12: Complaints about a recruitment decision
items.source: Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: If you think a competition breached the Recruitment Principles, you can complain, but the route and the ground matter. Start by identifying what actually went wrong: a vacancy that should have been advertised, a panel member with an undeclared relationship, criteria that changed, different treatment of candidates, or a refusal of a reasonable adjustment. A low score you disagree with is not, by itself, a breach, because panels have discretion over marks. Collect facts: dates, communications, who said what and the advert. Read the department's complaints procedure, which is usually on the Civil Service Jobs page or in the candidate pack, and follow its steps and time limits. Write a clear complaint that states what happened, which principle you believe was breached and what outcome you want, and keep the tone factual. The department should investigate impartially, often through someone not involved in the original decision, and respond in writing. If you remain dissatisfied, you may take the matter to the Civil Service Commission, which considers whether the Principles were breached, normally after the department process is complete and within a time limit. Separate routes exist if you believe you were discriminated against, and these have their own time limits. Keep a record of everything, avoid public accusations, and consider whether you want to remain in the process or move on.

questions.prompt: What should you do first before making a recruitment complaint?

options.text: Contact panel members privately and ask them to explain their scores
Post about the issue publicly so the department is pressed to respond
Ask for the winning candidate's score so you can compare it with yours
Identify what actually went wrong in the process

questions.prompt: Which is a genuine ground for a recruitment complaint?

options.text: A dislike of the interview style or the way the questions were put
A post filled without advert where the Principles required one
A delay of one working day in sending out the outcome
A mark that you think should have been higher on one answer

questions.hint: A breach of principle is needed.

questions.prompt: Why is disagreeing with a mark not usually a breach?

options.text: Panels have discretion over marks provided the process was fair
Marks are set by law and cannot be questioned by candidates or departments
Marks cannot be reviewed under any circumstances once the panel has signed
Marks are agreed with each candidate before the outcome is sent

questions.hint: Discretion is allowed within a fair process.

questions.prompt: Where do you usually find a department's complaints procedure?

options.text: On panel members' own pages when they take part in a competition
In the national press when a competition is reported on
In the candidate pack or on the Civil Service Jobs page
In a Cabinet Office handbook that only senior staff are allowed to read

questions.prompt: What should a good complaint include?

options.text: A detailed account of the faults of the other candidates in the process
A demand for an apology and compensation, whatever the facts show
What happened, which principle was breached and the outcome you want
A full list of your qualifications and awards to show why you deserved the post

questions.prompt: Who should investigate a complaint within a department?

options.text: Someone not involved in the original decision
The candidate who made the complaint, working with the panel
The chair of the original panel, who understands the decision best
The line manager of the post being recruited to, who wants it filled

questions.prompt: When may a candidate take a complaint to the Commission?

options.text: At any time in the future, as no time limit applies to complaints
After the department's process is complete and within a time limit
Only if the department agrees in writing to the Commission being involved
Straight away, before the department has had a chance to reply to you

questions.prompt: What does the Commission examine?

options.text: Whether the panel members personally liked the person who complained
Whether the complainant deserved the post on the strength of their service
Whether the winning candidate was a better person than the complainant
Whether the Recruitment Principles were breached

questions.prompt: A candidate believes they were discriminated against. What applies?

options.text: A route exists only for civil servants who already hold a post
Only the Commission can act, whatever time has passed
A separate route that has its own time limits
Only the panel can look at it, once the outcome has been issued

questions.prompt: What should you avoid while a complaint is in progress?

options.text: Writing factually and keeping to the point of the breach
Asking for the department's response to be given in writing
Keeping a record of what happened and when it took place
Public accusations

questions.hint: Public accusations can harm the process.

items.title: L12: Reading feedback after a near-miss
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: A near-miss, where you were close to the pass mark or just below the successful candidates, gives the most useful feedback. Departments commonly report scores for each criterion and sometimes a short note on strengths and areas for development. Read the scores in context: was your lowest score on the lead behaviour, or on a minor criterion? Note whether your marks were consistent or whether one weak area pulled you down. Where the feedback is in a banded form, such as meeting the standard or not, ask what a higher band would look like. Look for causes rather than symptoms: a low score on Communicating and Influencing could stem from unclear structure, lack of outcome, or too little detail about your own role. Compare feedback from this and earlier competitions to see if the same point recurs. If you were placed on a reserve list, you have shown the standard, and the difference between you and those appointed may be small. Do not interpret one near-miss as evidence you are not ready; equally, do not assume that persistence alone will change the result. Decide what to change: target a different type of post, build the missing evidence or improve the delivery. Ask a colleague who has been successful to read your written answers, and practise the interview with someone who will give honest feedback. Then set a date for the next application so that the learning is applied.

questions.prompt: Which type of feedback is the most useful to analyse?

options.text: A candidate pack with no scores and no comments at all
Feedback from a near-miss close to the pass mark
Feedback from another candidate who has already been successful
Feedback from a very low score, which shows exactly what to avoid

questions.hint: Near-misses show small changes can matter.

questions.prompt: What should you check about your scores?

options.text: Whether your lowest mark was on a lead criterion or a minor one
Whether the panel was larger than usual and so more reliable
Whether other candidates had similar feedback to yours in the same competition
Whether you scored highest on every criterion, as that proves fitness

questions.prompt: A low score on Communicating and Influencing could come from

options.text: Arriving a few minutes late on the day of a remote interview
Unclear structure, missing outcomes or too little about your own role
Wearing clothes that the panel judged unsuitable for a senior post
A weak handshake or an informal manner when you entered the interview room

questions.prompt: How does banded feedback help?

options.text: By removing the need for any improvement before the next application
By proving the panel was unfair in the way it banded candidates
By asking what a higher band would look like
By publicly ranking all candidates so that you can compare yourself

questions.prompt: What does a reserve list place tell you?

options.text: You showed the standard and the gap to appointed candidates may be small
You will certainly be appointed to the next suitable vacancy that arises
You failed the competition but may re-sit it at a later date
You are barred from reapplying to the same department for a year

questions.hint: Reserve means success without a post.

questions.prompt: Why compare feedback across competitions?

options.text: To decide which candidate was the cleverest across all the competitions
To choose which department to avoid applying to in future
To prove that the panels in each competition were wrong in their marking
To find points that recur

questions.prompt: Is one near-miss evidence that you are not ready?

options.text: It is conclusive if the winner was less experienced than you
It is conclusive, since the pass mark is an absolute measure of ability
It is conclusive, as panels are never wrong about readiness
It is limited evidence, as small differences can decide the outcome

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a good response to a near-miss?

options.text: Applying again without changing anything
Building the missing evidence through stretch work or a loan
Targeting a different type of post that suits your evidence better
Improving the way you deliver written and spoken answers

questions.prompt: Who is best placed to review your written answers?

options.text: The panel member who scored you, since they know your answers best
A colleague who has been successful in similar competitions
A recruiter from outside government who reviews private-sector applications
A person who has no knowledge of the Civil Service and so cannot be biased

questions.prompt: What makes learning from feedback effective?

options.text: Waiting for the perfect vacancy to appear before reviewing the feedback
Repeating the same answers in the next competition to show consistency
Setting a date for the next application to apply it
Keeping the feedback private and not looking at it again
